figures.shows: Schematic of the VQLS loop: a quantum computer block (ancilla Hadamard, ansatz V(alpha), state-preparation U, box F(A), measurements) returns the cost C(alpha) to a classical computer block that minimizes it and sends parameters alpha back; if C is at most gamma the loop ends and outputs alpha_opt. Input box: A as a sum of unitaries A_l and U with U|0> = |b>. Output box: circuit V(alpha_opt) prepares |x>.
figures.confirmed_by: The output of VQLS is a quantum state |x⟩ that is approximately proportional to the solution of the linear system Ax = b.

figures.shows: Cost function (y, log scale from about 0.001 to 1) against number of cost function evaluations (x, 0 to about 5 x 10^4) for kappa = 20. Blue curves are the local cost CL and red curves the global cost CG, for n = 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 (legend labels at the right edge). The local cost for n = 10 reaches about 0.001 at about 3 x 10^4 evaluations; the n = 50 local cost ends near 0.01 to 0.02; the global cost for n = 50 stays near 1 and the global cost falls more slowly as n grows.
figures.confirmed_by: At n = 50, our optimization cannot significantly lower CG below a value of one.

figures.shows: Layered Hardware-Efficient Ansatz on n = 10 qubit wires with four layers: columns of single-qubit Ry gates alternating with controlled-Z gates on alternating pairs of neighboring qubits; a dashed box marks one layer.
figures.confirmed_by: The number of variational parameters and gates scales linearly with n: for n = 50, four layers of this ansatz consist of 640 gates and 440 variational parameters.

figures.shows: Time-to-solution (y, 0 to about 5 x 10^4) against condition number kappa (x, about 20 to 200) for the Ising-inspired QLSP; solid lines epsilon = 0.002, dashed lines epsilon = 0.01; blue n = 10, red n = 20, green n = 30. All curves rise slowly with kappa. At kappa = 200 the epsilon = 0.002 curves reach about 1.5 x 10^4 (n = 10), about 3.2 x 10^4 (n = 20) and about 4.7 x 10^4 (n = 30).
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 4 shows that as the condition number κ is increased, the time-to-solution needed to achieve a given ϵ increases with a scaling that appears to be sub-linear.

figures.shows: Time-to-solution (y, 1 to 5 x 10^4) against 1/epsilon (x, about 100 to 900) for the Ising-inspired QLSP, n = 10, 20, 30 (blue, red, green), kappa = 60 (solid) or 200 (dashed); an inset shows the same data with a logarithmic x axis, where the curves are close to straight lines. Growth is slow and concave on the linear axis.
figures.confirmed_by: These results show that as 1/ϵ grows, the time-to-solution exhibits a logarithmic growth.

figures.shows: Time-to-solution (y, about 0.5 x 10^4 to about 3 x 10^4) against number of qubits n (x, 6 to 30) for epsilon = 0.01 and kappa = 60 (blue), 120 (red), 200 (green) for the Ising-inspired QLSP; the curves rise close to linearly with n. At n = 30 the values are about 1.9 x 10^4, about 2.4 x 10^4 and about 3.1 x 10^4.
figures.confirmed_by: As the number of qubits increases the time-to-solution needed to guarantee a particular ϵ with κ fixed appears to increase linearly with n.

figures.shows: Three panels for random matrices. a) log-log time-to-solution (y, about 4 x 10^5 to 3 x 10^7) against kappa (x, 10 to about 160) for n = 4 with epsilon = 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3 and power-law fits labeled about kappa^0.94, kappa^0.97, kappa^0.98 and kappa^0.81. b) time-to-solution (y, 0 to 3.5 x 10^7) against 1/epsilon (x, log scale 3 to 10^4) for kappa = 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 with linear fits. c) log-log time-to-solution (y, about 10^3 to 10^7) against n (x, 2 to 7) for epsilon = 0.3 and kappa = 10, with a fit labeled n^8.5.
figures.confirmed_by: In all cases we found m < 1, indicating that the scaling in κ for these examples is at worst linear.

figures.shows: Cost CG (y, 0 to 1) against iteration (x, 0 to about 150) for a simulator curve labeled QVM (black) and two hardware runs labeled Aspen-7-10Q-B Run 1 (red) and Run 2 (green). papers.what_it_is: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm (VQLS) for the quantum linear systems problem, with cost functions, a proved precision bound, a DQC1-hardness result, noise-resilience proofs, numerical scaling studies up to 50 qubits and Rigetti hardware runs up to 10 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors report that, using Rigetti's quantum computer, they successfully implement VQLS up to a problem size of 1024 × 1024.
quotes: Using Rigetti’s quantum computer, we successfully implement VQLS up to a problem size of 1024 × 1024.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical hardware result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 1024 x 1024 run uses a very structured matrix and a product-state ansatz of single-qubit Ry gates (Section 2.3), so it shows the cost can be trained on hardware for that case, not a general solver at that size.

assertions.value: The paper proves that the global cost function CG is at least epsilon squared divided by kappa squared, where epsilon is the trace distance to the exact solution and kappa is the condition number of A, assuming the first excited state of the effective Hamiltonian is non-degenerate (the authors state the same proof approach works for the degenerate case).
quotes: Inserting this into (13) yields CG ⩾ ϵ2/κ2.
By construction |x0⟩ is the ground state of HG with E0 = 0. In what follows we assume for simplicity that |x1⟩ is non-degenerate, although the same proof approach works for the degenerate case.
Additionally, we assume κ < ∞
and ||A|| ⩽ 1, and that the Al unitaries can be implemented with efficient quantum circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper proves the bound in Section 2.1.3, p.4, and the conditions are quoted from Section 2.1.1 and the proof; the proof uses a cited lower bound on the first excited energy (see the separate assertion).
assertions.reader_inference: The degenerate case is stated to follow by the same approach but is not written out.

assertions.value: The paper uses, citing Ref. [8], that the first excited state energy of the effective Hamiltonian is at least 1/κ squared, where κ is the condition number.
quotes: and that the first excited state energy satisfies E1 ⩾ 1/κ2 (which was shown in Ref. [8])
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The precision bound of the preceding theorem depends on this cited result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the remaining inequalities of the precision bound, for the local and the unnormalized cost functions, follow from the bound relating local and global costs and from the inner product of A applied to x with itself being at most 1.
quotes: The remaining inequalities in (9) follow from (8) and from the fact that ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ ⩽ 1, which
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper derives these bounds in Section 2.1.3, p.4, from the proved relation in Appendix B.

assertions.value: The authors state that the operational meaning of the cost functions as upper bounds gives a termination criterion for VQLS that guarantees a desired precision epsilon.
quotes: This is crucial since it gives a termination criterion for VQLS that guarantees a desired precision ϵ.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary statement of the authors that rests on the bound entered separately; no limit of its own.
assertions.reader_inference: The criterion needs the cost value, and its guarantee is only as tight as the bound allows: the hardware runs in the supplement reach a cost that gives a trivial bound.

assertions.value: The paper defines the error tolerance epsilon as the trace distance between the exact solution state and the approximate solution state prepared with the optimal parameters.
quotes: is the trace distance between the exact solution |x0⟩ and the approximate solution |x(αopt)⟩.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines epsilon in Section 2.1.1, p.3.

quotes: Furthermore, one can employ the operational meaning of the trace distance [39] to note that, for any POVM element M , we have ϵ ⩾ D(M ), where
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as a cited property of trace distance without a proof of its own.

assertions.value: The paper proves that all four VQLS cost functions are faithful: they are non-negative and vanish if and only if A applied to |x⟩ equals |b⟩.
quotes: Therefore, all four cost functions are faithful, vanishing if and only if A|x⟩ = |b⟩.
We assume that κ is not infinite (i.e., that A is full rank) and hence that ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ ̸= 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix B, p.11, with the full-rank condition quoted from Section 2.1.2, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper writes the vanishing condition as equality in Appendix B and as proportionality (A applied to x proportional to b) in Section 2.1.2; the normalization differs between the cost functions.

assertions.value: The paper proves that each local cost function is at most the corresponding global cost function, and each global cost function is at most n times the corresponding local cost function, where n is the number of qubits.
quotes: This implies that CG ⩾ CL and CG ⩾ CL.
Hence we have nHL ⩾ HG, which implies nCL ⩾ CG and nCL ⩾ CG.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix B, p.11, with both directions quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. [38], that global cost functions can exhibit barren plateaus, meaning cost function gradients that vanish exponentially in the number of qubits n.
quotes: We emphasize that global cost functions such as those in (3) and (5) can exhibit barren plateaus, i.e., cost function gradients that vanish exponentially in the number of qubits n, see Ref. [38].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Proposition 1) that the problem of estimating the VQLS cost functions to within precision of inverse polynomial in n is DQC1-hard.
assertions.anchor: Proposition 1, Section 2.1.5, p.5; Appendix D, p.13
quotes: to within precision ±δ = 1/ poly(n) is DQC1-hard.
Moreover, it is known that approximating ∆HS to within inverse polynomial precision is DQC1hard [33], and hence the result follows.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix D, p.13, by reduction; the statement and its precision condition are quoted from p.5 and the reduction relies on a cited DQC1-hardness result [33].
assertions.reader_inference: The hardness is for estimation to inverse-polynomial additive precision on specific instances built from the reduction (A equal to the identity), not for every VQLS problem instance.

assertions.value: The authors state that classically simulating DQC1 is impossible unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses to the second level, citing other work.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author's inference that rests on a complexity-theoretic assumption; the paper says it strongly suggests, not proves.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardness covers estimation of the cost for worst-case instances; the heuristic scaling runs in the paper are simulated classically for up to 50 qubits for structured problems.

assertions.value: The paper defines Optimal Parameter Resilience (OPR): a cost function exhibits OPR to a noise model if the noise does not shift the global minima in parameter space, so the optimal parameters are not changed by the noise.
quotes: A cost function exhibits OPR to a given noise model if this noise does not shift the global minima in parameter space, i.e., if the optimal parameters are not changed by the noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definition it uses in Appendix G, p.15 (taken from Ref. [60]).

assertions.value: The paper proves that the normalized global cost function has the same minimizing parameters with and without global depolarizing noise, that is, it exhibits OPR, under the assumptions that noise affects the real and imaginary parts to an equal extent and that circuit depth is dominated by the ansatz.
quotes: Let us first consider global depolarizing noise, which
We assume noise affects the estimation of the real and imaginary parts of
the depth of the circuit will likely be dominated by
This proves our desired statement of OPR, since it shows that the optimal parameters are unaffected by the noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix G.1, p.15, with the noise model and the assumptions quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof assumes the number of circuit layers is the same for all terms of the cost and that the maximally mixed state gives zero expectation; real devices may violate these.

assertions.value: The paper proves OPR for the normalized local cost function under global depolarizing noise, and states that the normalized local cost also exhibits OPR for noise that includes both global depolarizing noise and symmetric measurement noise.
quotes: Hence we have proven OPR for C˜L under global depolarizing noise.
This means that C˜L exhibits OPR to a noise model that includes both global depolarizing as well as symmetric measurement noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix G.2, p.16, under the stated assumptions; the statement is quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof notes the faithfulness property corresponds to OPR assuming the ansatz can express the true solution.

assertions.value: The authors state that they consider only relatively simple noise models, global depolarizing noise and measurement noise, and leave more complicated noise models for future work.
quotes: We leave the analysis of more complicated noise models for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit on its own noise analysis in Appendix G, p.15.

assertions.value: The authors state that the procedure based on probabilistic error cancellation shows that, with polynomial overhead, one can verify whether the solution is optimal by satisfying the termination conditions.

assertions.reader_inference: The argument also requires the gates of the device to form a basis for the unitary operations (quoted on p.6) and the overhead includes the negativity gamma, whose size is not bounded in the paper.
